ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Gynecologic Oncology Consultation — Ada Lovelace — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week follow-up and gynecologic oncology consultation: pathology, MRI and PET-CT, staging, treatment intent, palliative care, and long-acting morphine

text.paragraph: Friable exophytic cervical mass with five months of abnormal bleeding and constant pelvic pain in a 35-year-old woman, biopsied today, with iron deficiency anemia. Please confirm the diagnosis, stage the disease, advise on treatment intent and options, and help with control of bleeding and pain. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks; pathology expected within a week. [S]

list.item: What is the diagnosis, and what further staging is needed?
Is the intent of treatment curative or palliative, and what treatment do you recommend?
How should the bleeding be controlled?
Which tumor or genetic tests are needed?
How should her pain and long-term opioid therapy be managed during treatment?
When should palliative care be involved?

text.paragraph: Mrs. Lovelace, a 35-year-old mathematician, is seen at the request of Dr. Whitley-Adeyemi for a cervical mass found two weeks ago after five months of abnormal bleeding and pelvic pain. The bleeding is lighter since the first iron infusion but continues. Her pain averages 6 of 10 on oral morphine solution 5 mg about six times a day, without drowsiness; she stopped the opium tincture she had taken for two years. She has no cough, hemoptysis, bone pain, leg swelling, or urinary or bowel symptoms beyond opioid-related constipation. She has never had cervical screening. She does not wish to preserve fertility. She asked to be told the findings directly. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Augusta Ada Byron was born on December 10, 1815, in Piccadilly, London, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron and Anne Isabella Byron. [D]
She was often ill as a child. In 1829, at 13, she caught measles, from which she took a long while to recover; she was bedridden for a whole year. [D]
On July 8, 1835, she married William King, who was created an earl in 1838, making her Countess of Lovelace. [D]
Her health suffered after a bout of cholera in 1837, and she had lingering problems with asthma and her digestive system. [D]
Her doctors gave her painkillers such as laudanum and opium; she reportedly had mood swings and hallucinations. [D]

Between 1842 and 1843 she translated L. F. Menabrea's article on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and added her own extensive Notes, published in 1843 under the initials A.A.L. The Notes, which include a method for computing Bernoulli numbers on the engine, are often described as the first published computer program. [D]

Her health, always fragile, declined sharply after 1843. By the end of that year she was taking several medicines for different health problems; in 1844 she wrote that a recent illness had left her 'utterly unable to think even of my studies', and she thought of writing a scientific study of the effects of opium and wine based on her own experience. In the 1840s she had what she called heart or rheumatic attacks. [D]
Gambling on horses was a passion of her later years, and she pawned some of her jewels to finance it. [D]
By 1851 she was extremely sick with uterine cancer. [D]

list.item: Adenocarcinoma of the cervix, HPV 18 positive, FIGO 1843 stage IVB by imaging (C53.0). The lung nodules and para-aortic nodes on PET-CT mean distant spread, stage IVB by imaging; because this decides that treatment is palliative rather than curative, a lung nodule should be biopsied to confirm it before systemic therapy. With PD-L1 combined positive score 5, the NCCN preferred first-line treatment is carboplatin or cisplatin with paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, with or without bevacizumab, based on KEYNOTE-826. I recommend carboplatin, for ease and less toxicity, and leaving out bevacizumab for now, because she is bleeding from the tumor and will have pelvic radiation, which raise the risks of hemorrhage and fistula. Cervical cancer is not part of a hereditary cancer syndrome, so germline testing is not indicated; the tumor biomarkers are complete for first-line and later choices. [S]

Iron deficiency anemia from tumor bleeding (D50.0). Bleeding will not stop without treating the tumor. A short course of palliative pelvic radiation controls bleeding in most patients within one to two weeks. Transfusion if hemoglobin falls below 7 to 8 g/dL or she has symptoms. [S]

Cancer-related pelvic pain (G89.3). Constant visceral and nociceptive pain from the tumor and parametrial spread, needing scheduled opioid therapy, which radiation and systemic treatment should also reduce. Her long prior use of opium tincture does not argue against opioids for cancer pain, but calls for clear, measured dosing, one prescriber, and attention to sedation, given her wish for a clear mind. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Cervical biopsy: invasive adenocarcinoma, usual (HPV-associated) type, p16 diffusely positive, HPV 18 detected; PD-L1 combined positive score 5; mismatch repair proteins retained; HER2 immunohistochemistry 1+. Pelvic MRI a week ago: 5.2 cm endocervical tumor with left parametrial invasion, not reaching the sidewall, no hydronephrosis, an enlarged left external iliac node. FDG PET-CT five days ago: avid tumor, avid left pelvic and para-aortic nodes, six avid nodules in both lungs up to 1.4 cm, no bone or liver lesions. Hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL today, from 8.4; creatinine 0.66 mg/dL; ALT 17 U/L; TSH 1.9 mIU/L; HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C tests negative. [S]

list.item: CT-guided biopsy of a lung nodule to confirm metastatic disease. [S]
Palliative pelvic radiation, 20 Gy in 5 fractions, starting next week, for bleeding and pain. [S]
Then carboplatin (AUC 5), paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 and pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks for six cycles, with pembrolizumab continuing as maintenance; no bevacizumab for now. [S]
Blood counts, creatinine and ALT before each cycle; TSH and free T4 at baseline and every six weeks on pembrolizumab; restaging CT after four cycles. [S]
No germline genetic testing. [S]

Long-acting morphine 15 mg every 12 hours with morphine solution 5 mg as needed for breakthrough pain, a daily bowel regimen, naloxone, and one prescriber, under Dr. Whitley-Adeyemi with the palliative care team. [S]
Specialist palliative care alongside treatment from today. [S]
Complete intravenous iron; transfuse only below 7 to 8 g/dL or for symptoms. [S]

Dr. Whitley-Adeyemi and I gave Mrs. Lovelace the diagnosis together, at her request, in plain words: the cancer has spread and cannot be cured, and treatment aims to stop the bleeding, ease the pain, control the cancer and help her live longer and well. She asked about treatment and its effects on her thinking, and chose radiation and chemotherapy with pembrolizumab. The palliative care team saw her the same afternoon. [S]
Follow-up: Gynecologic oncology after the lung biopsy and before the first cycle, then before each cycle, with restaging after four cycles. [S]
